content: White mustard, scientifically known as Sinapis alba, is an annual plant belonging to the family Cruciferae. It is also sometimes referred to as Brassica alba, B. hirta, or yellow mustard. This plant is cultivated for various purposes, including its seeds (used as mustard), as a fodder crop, or as green manure. Although it is now grown worldwide, it is believed to have originated in the Mediterranean region. The plant produces yellow flowers that develop into hairy seed pods. Each pod typically contains about six seeds. These seeds are harvested just before the pods ripen and burst. White mustard seeds are small, hard, and round, measuring approximately 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter. Their color ranges from beige or yellow to light brown. The seeds can be used whole, such as in pickling, or toasted to enhance their flavor in culinary dishes. When ground and combined with other ingredients, they can be made into a paste or a more conventional mustard condiment. The seeds of white mustard contain a compound called sinalbin, a thioglycoside that contributes to their characteristic pungent taste. Compared to black mustard seeds, white mustard seeds have fewer volatile oils, resulting in a milder flavor profile.
